extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of psychology and philosophy (lecture attendees)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating metaphysical and psychological theories about the composition/unity of consciousness — their logical coherence, empirical plausibility, use of analogy, and imaginative power. Focus is on how to judge claims that higher minds or collective minds relate to individual minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision / imaginative richness
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher's 'vision' or imaginative richness: e.g. 'Few professorial philosophers have any vision. Fechner had vision,' which makes his writing re-readable and yields a 'fresh sense of reality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to authors who provide vivid, concrete, and emotionally compelling pictures of their theory (Fechner's earth-soul imagery is praised). Anti-pattern: dry, purely rationalistic presentations that leave the account 'thin' and unpersuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailing intermediary stages of collectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should 'mark the various intermediary stages and halting places of collectivity' (e.g. relations: senses → individual mind → earth-soul → solar system → ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer accounts that trace intermediate forms and gates of approach rather than leaping directly from individuals to an absolute; concrete intermediary descriptions increase explanatory plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency / avoidance of self-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories must not be self-contradictory: James criticizes monistic idealists for attributing incompatible claims (e.g. treating parts and whole as strictly identical while also treating mental states as what they appear to be).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for formal contradictions (identity, individuation) and for covert equivocations. Anti-pattern: ignoring long-standing objections or logical barriers that undermine the central claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with psychological/phenomenological facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect that 'mental' existence is 'sentiri'/'experiri' — e.g. 'If I feel pain, it is just pain that I feel.' The theory must comport with how mental states actually present themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defensible metaphysical account should not conflict with basic psychological facts about experience and appearance; if it does, it must explicitly refute or reframe those facts rather than silently override them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a mechanism of unification (distinct agent vs mere sum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either explain how unification occurs without positing a separate agent (and avoid logical nonsense), or legitimately admit a distinct unifying agent (e.g. a theistic God or higher witness) rather than insisting the whole is numerically identical with its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the theory supplies a plausible unifying mechanism (how individual experiences become part of a collective awareness) instead of merely renaming a collection as a 'whole.' Anti-pattern: a 'joint-stock company all shareholders and no treasurer' — no account of who directs or unifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of emergent/new qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that higher collective states may be 'something new' (e.g. the thought of a sentence is not merely the sum of the thoughts of its words — 'there is something new in the collective consciousness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good accounts distinguish between mere aggregation and genuine emergence, allowing higher-level states to have properties not present in the elements. Anti-pattern: simplistic reduction that treats higher states as numerically identical with their parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candid engagement with objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should openly acknowledge and address significant objections and difficulties (James reproaches writers who 'passed them by in silence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the theorist notes counterarguments and attempts to refute them; failure to do so signals rhetorical rather than intellectual honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of metaphors and analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors (sentence, shower, bird, etc.) can illuminate but also seduce into error; they are 'beautiful' yet may mislead if overextended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metaphors for scope and limits; ensure analogies do not illegitimately transfer properties across categories. Anti-pattern: taking a felicitous metaphor as warrant for universal metaphysical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to qualitative differences across organisms/organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that different organizational forms (plants, animals, instruments) may have qualitatively different kinds of consciousness (e.g. Fechner's suggestion that plant consciousness could be 'of another type').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming a single model of consciousness fits all biological forms; good theories allow for modality-specific modes of feeling or awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory richness ('thickness') versus thin abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer accounts that render the universe 'thickly' articulated (rich in particulars and relations) rather than the 'thin' outlines of abstract rationalistic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value theories that supply concrete content, relations, and moral/religious access points; anti-pattern: elegant but content-poor universals that fail to connect with lived phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for physical/ontological category distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of importing physical-world notions of 'whole' into mental ontology without justification: in the physical world 'whole' is often only our name for a grouping, whereas in the mental world wholes can 'realize themselves per se.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the theorist does not illegitimately conflate physical grouping with genuine mental unity; require argument when moving between physical and mental analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenological fidelity (treat experiences as they present themselves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reinterpret away the given character of an experience: 'If I feel pain, it is just pain that I feel, however I may have come by the feeling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the account respects the presented nature of experiences; deviations from appearance require explicit argument and not mere metaphysical assertion.
